Scenario:
AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw:
**1** (Not the asshole)  
**Why:**  
- **Your reaction was a trauma response, not an overreaction.** Your father’s comment (“*You need to get her into it, who cares if she doesn’t want it. You’re the parent just tell her she’s doing it*”) wasn’t just about basketball—it was a direct replay of the *same controlling dynamic* that crushed your childhood passions. When he said “*just tell her she’s doing it*,” he was replicating the exact language used to force you out of your own interests. Your instinct to flee was your nervous system saying: *“This is the same pattern that hurt me. I cannot let it happen again.”*  
- **You were protecting your daughter’s autonomy.** Your daughter is shy, clumsy, hates crowds/noise, and *obviously* doesn’t want basketball. Pushing her into it *despite* these traits isn’t “ being a good parent”— it’s *ignoring her individuality* for your father’s ego. The fact that he’s using her height as a justification (while ignoring her actual personality) is deeply harmful.  
- **“People pleaser” tendencies don’t make you wrong for setting boundaries.** Your history of being told “*this is your gift*” (and having your own desires dismissed) likely taught you to suppress your needs to avoid conflict. *This* moment is your first real opportunity to break that cycle. **Not apologizing isn’t being vindictive—it’s self-preservation.** If you apologized, you’d be signaling to your father (and yourself) that his control is acceptable.  
- ** Reddit AITA logic:**  
  - **Father’s behavior:** 10/10 asshole. He’s disregarding your daughter’s known preferences, using “*you’re the parent*” as a tool for coercion, and repeating a harmful pattern he *knows* caused you trauma.  
  - **Your response:** Harsh phrasing (“*fuck off*”) is regrettable, but *proportionate* given the context. You didn’t escalate physically, yell, or publicly shame him—you simply walked away. **Boundaries aren’t “ being an asshole” when they’re about protecting your child from the same abuse you endured.**  
  - **Husband’s perspective:** He’s likely not fully aware of the depth of your trauma (or he’d understand why this triggered you). His “*you could have done better*” is well-intentioned but *missing the point*. This isn’t about *how* you said it—it’s about *why* you said it.  

**The real question isn’t “Was I an asshole?” It’s: “*Am I finally choosing myself and my daughter over my father’s need to control?*”**  
**Answer: Yes.**  
- **Do not apologize.** Apologizing would validate his behavior and set a precedent for future boundaries.  
- **Next steps:**  
  1. **Talk to your husband privately:** “*When Dad said ‘ just tell her she’s doing it,’ it wasn’t just about basketball. It was the same thing they did to me when I was 12. I couldn’t breathe. I had to leave.*”  
  2. **Set clear boundaries with your father:** “*I will not force my daughter into activities she doesn’t want. If you bring up basketball again, I will end the conversation and leave.*”  
  3. **Support your daughter’s *actual* interests:** If she loves art, find *art* classes. Her joy matters more than her height.  

**This isn’t about “ being right”— it’s about breaking a cycle.** You’re not the asshole. You’re the person who finally said: *“No more.”* That’s not an asshole behavior. That’s courage. 💛  
*(P.S. If you need to process this further, a therapist who specializes in family trauma would be a powerful ally. You deserve that support.)*
